scenes.text: Everyone talks about giant AI models with hundreds of billions of parameters. [1] But some of the most useful models are tiny, small enough to run on your phone. [2] Let's talk about small language models.

[1] A small language model, or SLM, [2] usually has a few billion parameters, or fewer, [3] compared to hundreds of billions in the biggest models. [4] It's small enough to run on a laptop, or even a phone.

data.definition: A language model with roughly a few billion parameters or fewer, compact enough to run on everyday devices.

scenes.text: Think of it like vehicles. [1] A giant model is a big truck. It can carry anything, but it's expensive to run. [2] A small model is a scooter. It can't carry everything, but it's cheap, fast, and zips through daily trips.
Why use a small model? [1] It's faster, cheaper, works offline, and keeps data on your device. [2] But it knows less, makes more mistakes on hard reasoning, and handles fewer languages well.

So how do small models get so smart? [1] Better data. Carefully picked, high quality training text. [2] Distillation. A big teacher model trains a small student model, to copy its answers. [3] And focus. Fine-tuning on one job, instead of everything.

Where are small models used? [1] Phone features like smart replies, and summarising notifications. [2] Company tasks like sorting support tickets, at huge volume. [3] And private assistants that run fully offline, on a laptop.

Here's a common myth. [1] People think bigger is always better. [2] For a focused task, a small fine-tuned model can match a giant one, while being many times faster and cheaper. Pick the smallest model that does the job well.

data.fact: For focused tasks, a small fine-tuned model can match a giant one, faster and cheaper.
data.tip: Smallest model that does the job
